paragraphs: When the flood receded, the first mulberry fields reappeared downstream of Ye. Torn mats and children’s cloth shoes hung in the branches, where mud marks stood higher than a grown man. Soldiers recovering the dead erected three rows of timber racks on the embankment. Clothing, names, and places of discovery each had their own thin register. By afternoon the clerks' wrists ached from writing.
When a man’s body was brought in, his hand was still closed around a wooden bowl. The character Guo had been carved into its base, and the rim had been worn pale.
An old woman rushed out of the crowd. Before looking at the face, she gathered the bowl against her breast. She wiped the rim twice with her sleeve, then bent to examine her son’s swollen wrist.
“He used this bowl when he was little,” she said.

The clerk asked for his name and home village. Halfway through her answer, the woman fell silent. An officer checking the relief-grain records of the armed rebels recognized Guo family stockade and opened another register. “Guo Shi drew two measures of grain from a porridge station set up by the men at the old palace.”
The woman clutched the bowl. Two children behind her hid in her skirts, too frightened even to cry.
“Are you going to count him as one of the rebels?”

The officer hesitated. A subordinate of the judicial court approached, river mud still clinging to the hem of his robe. Rather than lift his brush, he asked the two children, “When you went for porridge, did you see any weapons?”

The elder shook his head. There were guards in front of the shelter, he said, but no one had been allowed to take a knife inside. The younger showed his frostbitten hand and said he had carried only a bowl.

The judicial officer told the clerk to record the death as drowning, enter receipt of grain separately, and leave the dead man outside the investigation for now. He sent the children with their grandmother to the settlement shelter for cakes. The old woman’s eyes reddened, but she did not move.
“Sir, I’ve told the truth. They won’t come tomorrow and take the children away, will they?”
The officer produced a bamboo tally marked with his office number. “If anyone comes for them tomorrow morning, make him find me first at the southern office.”
Only then did the old woman bend to straighten the collar of her dead son.

Disputes like this spread through Ye. The retainers of former Yan noble houses had handed out grain; so had the Qin army’s public granaries. Powerful families had operated ferries along the waterways. Starving refugees had seen nothing beyond the steaming pots; none had asked first whose banner hung overhead. But once the waters fell, every county was busy asking who had boarded which boat and who had eaten whose bowl of gruel.

The southern prison was packed. The court’s original arrest order had named “old adherents plotting to restore Yan.” In the hands of village heads it often became simply “people of Yan.” In one village of more than 170 households, the flood had swept away the thirty-li stretch of highway, and a Yan flag had hung in the village for a single day. The county commandant entered everyone who had seen it on his suspect list. A young widow asked who would have watched her two children if she had gone into the floodwater to tear the flag down. The commandant could not answer.

Murong Chui visited the prison. When the jailer opened the door, the air inside was hardly fit to breathe. An old soldier with a broken leg lay on straw, the scars of his years in the army north of the Huai still visible. He asked why he had been detained. “The day someone raised that flag, the flood carried off my house. I neither helped nor reported him.”
“Why did you not report him?” the county commandant demanded.
“With this leg?” The old soldier moved it a little. “Lend me a horse and I’ll go report him now.”

Murong Chui called for an army physician and ordered the commandant to produce the testimony on which the arrest had been made. Apart from “saw a Yan flag,” the file contained nothing but the village head’s fingerprint.
“Send him home,” he said.
The commandant turned gray. “General, if we release them all and one genuine criminal escapes among them—”

“Keep those against whom you have arrows, weapons, granary accounts, or gate guards as witnesses. Investigate the rest properly. Lock every villager together, and the arsonists have a perfect place to hide.”

Pei Heng recorded what they had found in the prison. He did not abandon his inspection simply because Murong Chui had given an order. Instead, he proposed forwarding the original detention register to the censors for safekeeping, so the commandant could not change the statements tomorrow.

When the two emerged from the cells, dozens knelt outside the office. Some sought release for relatives, others accused neighbors of stealing grain. A child held a padded coat pierced by an arrow and said her father was no soldier of restored Yan, yet had died beneath the eastern gate. She spread out the coat and followed a county clerk, demanding the name of the unit that had fired.

Murong Chui bent to inspect the hole. The arrow had entered from behind. People must have run wildly that night, and no one could now say with certainty whose shot had struck him. He ordered the coat and the place where the body was found entered in the record.
Pei Heng asked quietly, “Can you find the answer for her?”
“I don’t know.”
His answer was barely audible, but the child heard. Holding the coat, she stared at him in bewilderment.

After renewed examination by the judicial court, the cases were finally divided among several registers. There was evidence that Murong Yu Huan had shot and wounded a gate guard during his attack on the eastern gate. An estate owner had hidden weapons and carried pine resin out before the granary fire; granary hands and cart drivers could testify. Han Yin had attended the night banquet and surrendered his contact lists, but there was no proof he had taken part in setting fire to the western granary. Master Feng had gone home after the feast and applied the following day to disband his estate retainers. As for refugees who had taken grain, crossed rivers, or been forced to build fences, each was questioned about what he or she had actually done.

The inquiries proceeded slowly, but spaces began opening in the prison. Those first released clutched travel papers from the office and still dared not unfold them before the city gates. They feared the patrols would call the papers forgeries; the guards worried that replacements on the next watch would not recognize the seal. Pei Heng therefore ordered each gate to copy the names and numbers of those released that day by the judicial court, post them in the courier house, and have literate sergeants announce them to every shift. Only by the third day did some of the needless crying at the gates subside.

By the time the reports from Ye reached Chang’an, the autumn chill was deep. Fu Rong brought testimony from the counties, accounts of fire damage at military granaries, and relief-grain ledgers, together with an unaltered book of records kept by the censors. Fu Hong drew out a page first. He saw Guo Shi’s name and, beside it, the entry for two underage children given millet cakes. He read to the end, rolled up the sheet, and passed it to the judicial court.

At court some ministers urged the execution of the former Yan royal clan to remove a future danger. From Xiangyang, Fu Pi submitted a memorial arguing that as long as the former Yan ruler lived in Chang’an, the people of old Yan had a banner they could raise. Fu Jian had chosen not to kill him for now, but the danger would remain. Several Di princes agreed and proposed moving every branch of the Murong family to Guanzhong.

Fu Rong stood a long time before replying. “Murong Yu Huan shot a gate guard. If military law condemns him, there is nothing to argue. But you propose removing the Murong clan. A ten-year-old pupil in the commandery school bears that name. So does a woman who rescued people from the levee. Where must they be moved?”
A minister of the imperial clan said, “Yield one step now, and a greater disaster will come later.”
Fu Rong turned to the judicial officer. “Has Han Yin’s case been decided?”
“Not yet. The witnesses from the western granary are still being questioned against one another.”
“Then it has not been decided.”

The hall grew quiet. Fu Jian had read the short letter Murong Wei sent to Hebei. The original had passed through several hands and one corner was damaged, but Murong Wei had acknowledged the handwriting. It did not contain the words “raise troops.” It asked after old friends and said that Daoxuan remembered his ancestors and should know his place.
“Summon him,” Fu Jian said.

Murong Wei had lived for years in Chang’an, attended banquets at great houses, and accompanied Fu Jian on hunting excursions when invited. Led into court now, he walked with the same measured steps, though his robe no longer bore the patterns of his lost kingdom. He bowed as a Qin minister and, when he rose, gave Fu Rong the slightest nod, as though this were another ordinary audience from former times.
“When you wrote that letter, did you know Hebei was flooding?” Fu Jian asked.
“I did.”
“Did you know men were gathering old troops and grain in your name as their former sovereign?”
Murong Wei waited a moment. “Some asked me to sign a summons. I did not.”
“Who asked?”
He remained silent.

Fu Jian instructed the judicial officer to hand him a deposition from a copyist in Han Yin’s household. Twice men had sought the impression of the old royal seal, and twice it was refused. A third time, a reply had been sent consisting only of greetings. Murong Wei finished reading and closed his eyes for a moment.
“Someone has used Our family name as an order to the army,” he said softly, still employing the royal pronoun of his former days.
Fu Jian heard it, but did not correct him.
“You knew they would do so.”
“Your Majesty took Yan and ordered this servant to live in Chang’an, with an annual stipend. But I cannot forbid the dreams of Yan’s people, even for Your Majesty.”
“I did not ask about your dreams.”
“Nor did I command them to raise an army.”
Fu Jian laid the letter between them. For a long while there was no sound in the hall, except the palace attendants behind the curtains replacing charcoal.

“If you had personally ordered the granary burned, I could not spare you today. We have no such evidence. But you knew others wanted to gather men in your name, and still sent this ambiguous letter to test Murong Chui. You wanted him to respond, yet would not write down what you wanted him to do.”

Murong Wei looked up. “There is an edict Your Majesty keeps in his heart and will never finish writing. When is all under Heaven to belong to Qin? When must the world cease to have kings of other surnames? Has Your Majesty ever written that clearly?”

Fu Jian stopped short. He remembered that evening on the northern bank of the Fei, when he had reined in his horse and so many people awaited a single command to cross the river. Had he acted on one moment’s impulse, Great Qin would long since have taken another shape.
“That edict, too, is one I dare not write lightly.”
Murong Wei seemed about to smile, but did not. “I once sat in the place of honor in Yan’s palace. Now even a letter comforting old friends must be judged in Qin’s hall.”
“You may write to comfort old friends. That is different from letting them believe you are waiting for troops.”

The judicial court found insufficient evidence that Murong Wei had personally authorized the killing of officials or the setting of fires. But he had maintained contacts as a former sovereign, concealed the identity of messengers, and had repeatedly been approached by military estate holders. The court proposed stripping his title and forbidding correspondence beyond his residence. Fu Jian approved, and in the name of dynastic security added lifelong confinement in a separate residence outside the palace, with visits and letters subject to joint approval by the Imperial Clan Office and the judicial court. He signed the punishment himself, slowly.
“Why does Your Majesty not execute him?” a minister finally asked.
Fu Jian laid down his brush and glanced at Murong Wei kneeling below the steps. In youth this man had ruled Yan; now his temples, too, were streaked with white.
“To kill a man requires evidence of a capital crime. By confining him in that residence today, I have already given him reason to remember me for the rest of his life.”
As Murong Wei was led past the imperial steps, he turned toward Fu Rong. “Does the Duke of Yangping think the same?”
“I want to find the other letter sent to the estate owner.”
“And if it is never found?”
“Then it can never be used to convict you.”
Murong Wei fell silent and followed his guards out of the hall.

The verdict went to Hebei, but the former ministers did not become loyal for that reason. Di officers resented the light punishment; powerful Xianbei families feared the court had at last moved against Murong Wei. Han villagers cared chiefly about when each irrigation channel would be repaired. On the busiest day before the sentence notices posted in Ye’s southern market, no rebel general was being executed: villagers had come with witnesses to supply the names of another group wrongly detained.

When Murong Chui returned to Chang’an to report, he carried the last two flood ledgers compiled by Pei Heng. Some urged Fu Jian to reward him with a new fief in Hebei for his relief work. Others petitioned that the former Prince of Wu be kept in the capital forever.
Fu Jian received him alone in a small hall.
“The old ministers in Ye hate you.”
“I watched some of them grow up.”
“Do you hate them?”

Murong Chui lowered his head. After a long while he said, “I remember Han Yin carrying a bloodstained letter for me. Now he sits in the old palace and counts the grain that might keep people alive outside the walls as supplies for an army to restore Yan. I no longer know whom I should hate.”
Fu Jian looked at the burn on his arm that had not yet healed. “Your relief accounts contain more than six thousand measures issued before they were entered, to households not yet fully verified.”
“I accept responsibility.”
“You also gave former ministers private permission to leave the commandery. People are talking.”

“I submitted a full record to the inspector that night. They were permitted to travel only with county documents, and without weapons. If anyone crossed the limits, I ask that the facts be investigated.”
“And you compelled the Han estates to provide boats?”
“They received government vouchers in compensation. I sent armed soldiers to their doors, which broke the existing rules for requisitioning vessels.”
Fu Jian spread the two account books before him. “Saving lives deserves credit. Credit does not erase the breaking of an order or gaps in the accounts.”

The final decision commended Murong Chui but docked six months of his stipend; the missing relief entries were to be examined further. The relief units returned to their original garrisons. No personal army would be established for him in Hebei. Murong Chui asked to retain physicians and craftsmen who knew the rivers for another month to repair the levees. Fu Jian approved and ordered officers from the capital to take charge.
“If you want land in Hebei, you may ask for it today,” Fu Jian said.
Murong Chui shook his head. “When I heard them calling me Prince of Wu in Ye, I understood what another piece of land might set in motion. My stipend is enough to maintain my household.”
Fu Jian nodded slowly. “Then I have one less worry.”

At the first thaw after winter, the boundaries of the fields south of Ye were marked anew. Tuoba Lin led his wife and children to the county office and laid an old Yan horse tally on the table. For three generations his family had tended horses for an estate owner. Of the produce from the twenty mu he worked, six parts in ten went to the estate, and the land itself stood as security for a debt incurred buying fodder for oxen.

The county magistrate now assigned him thirty mu: the original twenty, plus ten adjoining mu of abandoned land verified to have no owner. Several unlawful high-interest charges were struck out, and rent was remitted for the flood year. While the county assistant read the terms aloud, Tuoba Lin dared not lift his head. When the reading was over, he asked again, “If the person who governs the fields changes, will this still count?”
The assistant said copies would be kept by both county and commandery and checked against the new Qin household registers. Tuoba Lin asked another question: “What if war comes and the papers burn?”

The assistant had no answer. At last he directed him to the new stone boundary markers, and said neighboring landholders and village elders could be called to attest in any dispute. Still uncertain, Tuoba Lin pressed his thumbprint onto the deed.

That day a hard wind blew along the riverbank, and a line of new markers emerged from the gray-white muddy fields. Tuoba Lin crouched at the edge of his plot and picked up a rusty Yan coin. He washed it and put it inside his robe. His wife asked why he wanted to keep it. He said he did not know; he would show it to their son when the boy grew older.

In the distance a few old men of Yan stood beside a collapsed estate wall, talking about the former palace. One said the people of Yan would return someday; another said they never would. Tuoba Lin listened for a while, then bent again to pile earth along his field ridge. The water between two boundary stones had not yet drained. He needed to dig a shallow ditch before dark so the spring planting would not rot again.
